title: 1 Samuel 14:16–23
context: 1 Samuel 14:16–23 describes the spread of the Philistine rout. Saul’s watchmen see the enemy camp melting away; a muster reveals that Jonathan and his armor bearer are missing. Saul begins to inquire of God through the priest Ahijah but breaks off as the tumult grows, and he leads his men into battle, where the Philistines are striking one another. Hebrews who had sided with the Philistines switch sides, and Israelites who had hidden join the pursuit. The narrator’s summary is clear: “So the LORD saved Israel that day.”

verses.text: The watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked; and behold, the multitude melted away and scattered.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul’s watchmen see “the multitude melted away and scattered.” Arminian readers note that the effects of Jonathan’s faith and God’s intervention become visible to the whole camp. Saul, who had been sitting still, now has an opportunity to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the melting of the enemy echoes the language used of Israel’s fear elsewhere, now reversed against the Philistines. God turns the tables. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the moment when the LORD’s deliverance becomes evident, preparing for Saul’s response.

verses.text: Then Saul said to the people who were with him, “Count now, and see who is missing from us.” When they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor bearer were not there.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul orders a count and finds Jonathan and his armor bearer missing. Arminian readers note that Saul seeks to understand events through an administrative check, which reveals that the victory began with his son’s faith rather than his own leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the count highlights Saul’s distance from what God is doing. The king learns of the victory after the fact. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the contrast between Saul and Jonathan, and neither finds a doctrinal question in the detail.

verses.text: Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring God’s ark here.” For God’s ark was with the children of Israel at that time.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul tells Ahijah, “Bring God’s ark here,” for the ark was with Israel at that time. Arminian readers note that Saul seeks to inquire of God, a right impulse in itself. Earlier the narrative mentioned Ahijah “wearing an ephod” (14:3), the priestly means of inquiry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s desire to consult God is commendable, but the following verse shows him breaking off before receiving an answer. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing Saul’s religious instincts, and both note that the narrative will question whether he truly waits on God’s word.

verses.text: While Saul talked to the priest, the tumult that was in the camp of the Philistines went on and increased; and Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand!”
verses.arminianNotes: As the tumult increases, Saul tells the priest, “Withdraw your hand!” Arminian readers note that Saul interrupts his inquiry because events seem to make it unnecessary. Impatience again overrides waiting on God, as at Gilgal in 13:8–9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the pattern: Saul starts to seek God but acts before God answers. Outward religion is joined to haste. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing a recurring weakness in Saul’s character, his tendency to act on circumstance rather than on God’s word.

verses.text: Saul and all the people who were with him were gathered together, and came to the battle; and behold, they were all striking each other with their swords in very great confusion.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul and his men come to the battle and find the Philistines “all striking each other with their swords in very great confusion.” Arminian readers note that the Israelites arrive to find the victory already underway. God’s action has done what Israel’s army could not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Gideon’s victory, where “the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow” (Judges 7:22). God defeats his enemies by turning them against one another. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the LORD as the true victor in the battle.

verses.text: Now the Hebrews who were with the Philistines before and who went up with them into the camp from all around, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
verses.arminianNotes: Hebrews who had been with the Philistines turn to join the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan. Arminian readers note that the turning tide of battle prompts people to change sides. Their return shows how God’s deliverance draws back those who had drifted away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reference to “Hebrews” with the Philistines suggests Israelites who had served or sided with the enemy. God’s victory regathers his scattered people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the widening deliverance, in which many share in a victory begun by a few.

verses.text: Likewise all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim, when they heard that the Philistines fled, even they also followed hard after them in the battle.
verses.arminianNotes: The Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim hear of the flight and join the pursuit. Arminian readers note that those who had hidden in fear in 13:6 now take courage. God’s action restores the courage of a fearful people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people join once the victory is evident, underscoring that the deliverance was God’s, begun through Jonathan’s faith. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the reversal of chapter 13, as the fearful people become pursuers.

verses.text: So the LORD saved Israel that day; and the battle passed over by Beth Aven.
verses.arminianNotes: “So the LORD saved Israel that day.” Arminian readers note that the narrator credits the victory to the LORD, not to Saul or even Jonathan. Jonathan’s faith was the occasion, but the LORD was the Savior. The same summary keeps Saul’s role modest, since the battle was already won before he arrived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the narrator’s theological summary, which confirms Jonathan’s confession in 14:6. The victory belongs to the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the heart of the episode, teaching that salvation belongs to the LORD and that he uses human faith and action to accomplish it.
